title: I lift up my eyes (Psalm 121)
hookLine: a pilgrim's song: my help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth

cards: Three times a year, the law of Moses called the people up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. For families far away that meant days on foot: dusty roads, children on shoulders, everyone singing to keep the pace.

And the city sits high in the hills, so the last stretch is always uphill. Fifteen psalms in a row, one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty-four, carry the same heading in the King James Bible: A Song of degrees.
Songs of going up. Some readers think pilgrims sang them on that road.

teach.b: Psalm one hundred twenty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."

It reads like a statement: my help comes from the hills. But the Hebrew can just as easily be read as a question, and many translations print it that way: I lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?
Why ask? The hills could be lovely, or they could be frightening. Bandits hid in them.

Some readers think of hilltop shrines to other gods, offering help of their own. Either way, the pilgrim looks up, and the next line answers: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth."
Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the voice changes.

Someone else seems to answer the pilgrim, maybe a friend on the road, maybe a priest: "He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber." Suffer means allow. Your foot won't slip on the path.
"Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep."

teach.h: KEEP, SIX TIMES IN EIGHT VERSES
teach.b: The King James Bible switches between keep and preserve, so the English hides it, but in Hebrew it is one verb, shamar, six times in eight verses. The one who keeps watches your coming and going, by day and by night.

teach.h: MY HELP COMETH FROM THE LORD.
teach.b: And the last verse: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Some Christians pray this psalm before a journey.

how: Many Christians pray Psalm 121 before a journey, and it is often read at funerals and at services of blessing for travelers, pilgrims and people leaving home.

o: to keep, to guard and watch over
to climb, to go up toward the city
to rest, to sleep when the night comes

games.q: you're a pilgrim on the road to Jerusalem, looking up at the hills. where does the psalm say your help comes from?
o: from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
games.why: "my help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." not from the hills, but from the one who made them.

practice: If you can see far, a skyline, a ridge, turn toward it and lift your eyes slowly, the way the pilgrim did; if you can't, picture the farthest place you've ever looked out over.

Ask the pilgrim's question quietly: where does my help come from? If you pray, answer with the psalm, my help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth; if you don't, just keep looking, and let the distance do its work.

wordCard.voice: Shamar. Hebrew for one who keeps and watches over, the word repeated six times in Psalm one hundred twenty-one.

orig.note: Hebrew: one who keeps, guards, watches over. its root appears six times in this eight-verse psalm.

carryVoice: Your line: my help comes. Your going out, and your coming in. Day four hundred thirty-three.
